approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail to the North Buttress
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct; west-side granite slab needs several rainless days before it is worth walking in for
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington take the Mountain Loop Highway southeast about 3 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 2060, the Clear Creek logging road, opposite the campground.

Drive roughly 6 miles up 2060. At about 5 miles the road forks and this is the decision that matters: bear RIGHT on the main fork for the Eightmile Creek trailhead. The LEFT fork is the Exfoliation Dome / Witch Doctor side of the same road system, several miles of driving away from anything on Three O'Clock Rock. Parking is on the left.

The trail climbs steeply through second growth, then levels into big old timber with some large cedars. After roughly 30-40 minutes it leaves the forest and starts across an old, partly overgrown talus slope. The path here is well built rather than a thrash — if you are fighting brush on the way in you are not on the Eightmile Creek trail.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stay on the main trail all the way across the talus. It runs straight into the rock, and where it touches the cliff is the low point of the North Buttress slab; the trail then continues along the base.

Standing at that contact point, look for a right-facing dihedral low on the slab with a single bolt roughly 20 feet above it. That bolt is the first piece of Silent Running. This is the central line up the shield of the North Buttress.

Negative marker: partway across the talus, about 100 feet before the trail reaches rock, a climbers' path branches up and LEFT into the slide maples. That branch is the South Buttress access (Great Arch, Big Tree). If you found yourself pushing uphill through maple brush you took it — come back down and keep going straight to where the trail hits the slab.
hazards: Talus slope crossing part-way along the trail — loose blocks under brush
Wrong fork at mile 5 on FR 2060 puts you on the Exfoliation Dome road instead

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, then the South Buttress branch
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
approach_variants.notes:
Drive as for the North Buttress: Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington, right onto FR 2060 (Clear Creek), about 6 miles up the road staying RIGHT at the fork near mile 5, park at the Eightmile Creek trailhead.

Walk the Eightmile Creek trail through second growth and then old timber, roughly 30-40 minutes, until it steps out of the forest onto the old talus slope.

The branch you want is easy to walk past. Once you are out of the woods, look LEFT within about the first 100 feet for a climbers' trail heading up and left into the slide maples. It is a boot path, not a built trail, and it is brushy from the start — that is normal here, not a sign you are wrong.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Buttress path pushes up through maple and hits rock at a prominent zig-zagging crack. That crack is the start of The Big Tree; you are on the South Buttress, home of the Great Arch.

Negative marker: if the trail took you all the way across the talus and ran into a clean slab with a single bolt above a right-facing dihedral, you are about 100 feet too far along — that is Silent Running on the North Buttress, a different formation face and a much harder day.
hazards: Unmarked, brushy climbers' path through slide maple
Talus slope with loose blocks hidden under vegetation

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, South Buttress branch to the Great Arch
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
approach_variants.notes:
As for The Big Tree — FR 2060 from the Mountain Loop Highway, right at the mile-5 fork, Eightmile Creek trailhead, then the Eightmile Creek trail for about 30-40 minutes to where it breaks out of the forest onto the talus.

Take the climbers' branch up and LEFT into the slide maples within roughly 100 feet of leaving the woods, and follow it to the South Buttress.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the first climb the South Buttress path brings you to, on the right-hand side of the Great Arch area — so if you have walked past several route starts you have gone too far.

The marker is a large left-facing flake with the first bolt on it. You can start on the flake itself or step onto it from just below. Above the flake the ground is low-angle slab past two more bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor, then three more bolts to anchors sitting below the roofs of the Great Arch.

Easy, low-angle friction off the deck is CORRECT here — this is the area's warm-up. If your first moves are steep or technical you are on one of the harder lines further along the Great Arch.
hazards: Unmarked brushy climbers' path through slide maple

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, South Buttress branch, then up to the terrace
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
approach_variants.notes: Drive and walk exactly as for the Great Arch: FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway, RIGHT at the mile-5 fork, Eightmile Creek trailhead, then the Eightmile Creek trail for 30-40 minutes to the talus slope, and the climbers' branch up and LEFT into the slide maples within about 100 feet of leaving the woods.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does NOT start where the approach path meets the rock. It starts from a terrace that sits between the Great Arch area and the start of The Big Tree, and the easiest way onto that terrace is from the Great Arch side.

So the sequence is: reach the Great Arch, then gain the terrace and walk along it toward the Big Tree side. If you are standing on the ground at the zig-zag crack you are at The Big Tree, not this route; if you are at the large left-facing flake with a bolt on it you are at Under the Bored Walk.

Having to scramble up onto a terrace before racking up is CORRECT here.
hazards: Unmarked brushy climbers' path through slide maple
Scrambling onto the terrace above the Great Arch

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail to the North Buttress, then traverse from Silent Running
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
approach_variants.notes: FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington, RIGHT at the mile-5 fork, park at the Eightmile Creek trailhead, and walk the built trail for 30-40 minutes through second growth and old timber until it steps onto the talus and runs into the North Buttress slab.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Revolver's five independent pitches are reached by traversing LEFT from Silent Running — it is not a line you walk up to on the ground and start.

So the base to find first is Silent Running's: the low point of the North Buttress slab where the trail touches rock, with a single bolt about 20 feet above a right-facing dihedral. From there the traverse leftward across the north slab gains this route.

If you are looking for an obvious independent ground start on the north slab and cannot see one, that is because there is not one.
hazards: Traversing terrain to reach the start — rope management on the leftward traverse

approach_variants.name: Granite Sidewalk to Blueberry Hill (west face)
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; the sidewalk is friction the whole way and is not worth attempting damp
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington head south and get onto FS 2060 (the Clear Creek road, also given as Frog Creek Road). Drive roughly 5 miles and take the LEFT fork — this is the opposite choice from the Three O'Clock Rock / Green Giant side of the same road, which is the right fork.

Carry on past the Witch Doctor pullout (about half a mile past the fork) and past the first washout. Park at the SECOND washout; that is the Blueberry Hill / Granite Sidewalk access.

Walk up a creek bed heading east for about 10 minutes until a continuous slab of granite of maybe 20 degrees runs uphill in front of you — this is the Granite Sidewalk. Go up the gully on the left to gain it, then climb the sidewalk for around 1,200 vertical feet to the base of the dome. It is walking and easy friction rather than a bushwhack, which is unusual for Darrington and is the sign you are on the right feature.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the top of the sidewalk a patch of trees marks the start of the Blueberry route, with a largish tree just below the patch. That tree is your reference point, and it is NOT your route.

From the largish tree, walk about 100-150 feet LEFT along the base and look for a single bolt. That bolt is the start of Dark Rhythm.

Negative marker: if you have racked up in or right at the tree patch you are on Blueberry Buttress. Dark Rhythm is a rope-length or so further left, and the only thing confirming it is the lone bolt.
hazards: Long unroped friction on the Granite Sidewalk — a slip has a long slide
Washouts on FS 2060 dictate where you can park; the drive-in point changes with road damage

approach_variants.name: Granite Sidewalk to Proxima Wall
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
approach_variants.notes:
FS 2060 south out of Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, then park at a small pullout on the west side of the road roughly 0.4 miles past the fork.

The approach follows the Granite Sidewalk — a long continuous low-angle granite ramp reached by walking up the creek bed east for about 10 minutes and then taking the gully on its left. Compared with a typical North Cascades approach this is close to schwack-free, and that is the confirmation you are on the sidewalk rather than in the timber beside it.

From the west slabs an approach gully leads to the base in roughly 20 minutes. Total from the car is about an hour to an hour and a half.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Proxima Wall faces west. The start is a bolted prow, and the specific thing to look for is a large Metolius bolt at the bottom of it.

A prow with a bolt on it is the marker — not a crack, not the tree patch. The tree patch at the top of the sidewalk belongs to Blueberry Buttress, and the single bolt 100-150 feet left of the tree below it belongs to Dark Rhythm; both are on Blueberry Hill, the same west face, and both are easy to mistake for this if you stop at the first thing you reach.
hazards: Long unroped friction on the Granite Sidewalk
Approach gully above the west slabs

approach_variants.name: Old logging grade and creek to Witch Doctor Wall (east face)
approach_variants.season: Dry summer; the wall is steep and east-facing, so it gets morning sun and dries earlier in the day than the slabs
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington head south onto FS 2060 (Clear Creek / Frog Creek Road), drive about 5 miles and take the LEFT fork. Roughly half a mile after the fork, just after crossing the bridge, there is a small pullout — that is the Witch Doctor access.

From the pullout walk a few metres along the road to where an overgrown old logging grade cuts back north-east into the forest on the left. Follow that old road for about a quarter mile to a switchback at a creek.

Leave the road there, enter the forest and pick up a faint climbers' path that handrails the creek. Keep the creek beside you for about 30 minutes until the boulder field and the wall come into view. Traverse the boulder field below the north side of the dome, then follow the wall southward.

Budget two hours, and closer to three if you lose the path — losing it here is common and is why the creek handrail matters more than any flagging.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are working south along the base of an east-facing wall that is unusually steep for Darrington. The base of the route sits just BEFORE a major gully, and that gully is on the left of the route as you face it.

The start itself is the obvious left-arching crack/flake. If you have walked into or past the major gully you have gone too far south; the arching flake is behind you.

Steep, non-slabby rock is CORRECT here. Witch Doctor Wall is the exception to the Darrington friction-slab character, so steepness is not evidence you are on the wrong formation.
hazards: Faint unmarked climbers' path — easy to lose, and route-finding failure is the normal way this approach goes wrong
Boulder field traverse below the north side of the dome
Creek crossing at the logging-road switchback

approach_variants.name: Witch Doctor approach continued to the far east end
approach_variants.season: Dry summer
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as Snake Charmer: FS 2060 south from Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, small pullout roughly half a mile past the fork just after the bridge, then the overgrown logging grade heading north-east into the forest, a switchback at a creek, and a faint path handrailing the creek to the boulder field beneath the dome.

Recorded times from the pullout are around 45 minutes to the first landmark and about an hour and a half of walking in total, carrying big loads.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This line sits on the FAR EAST end of the Witch Doctor Wall, on the section the first-ascent party called the Solar Wall — so you keep going past the ground below the arching flake of Snake Charmer.

The confirmation on arrival is two bivouac boulders sitting below the base of the wall, with a stream running behind that camp. If you are not standing near two obvious bivy rocks you have stopped short.

The climbing starts from Bombardier Ledge rather than from the deck.
hazards: Faint unmarked climbers' path
Boulder field beneath the wall
This is the aid-climbing end of the formation — loose blocks on the approach ledges

approach_variants.name: North Exfo approach to lower Salami Slab
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; these are west-facing friction slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Salami Slabs are the west-facing slabs below the north end of Exfoliation Dome, reached from the same FS 2060 (Clear Creek / Frog Creek Road) system as the rest of the dome — south from Darrington, and the LEFT fork at about 5 miles rather than the right fork that leads to Three O'Clock Rock.

The approach to lower Salami is an unmarked climbers' path and is described by locals as neither hard nor trivial; there is no maintained trail and no signage. The useful sighting aid is that the whole slab is plainly visible from Three O'Clock Rock across the valley, so pick the feature out from over there before you commit to the walk in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Snagglepuss starts exactly where the approach path reaches lower Salami Slab — arriving at the rock and finding yourself at the start of the route is the confirmation, not a coincidence.

It takes the heart of the slab: the first three pitches link slabby corridors to get over the prominent overlap and reach Salami Ledge. If the line above you does not run at the obvious overlap you are off to one side.

Negative marker: a long clean friction slab with almost no knobs, off to the RIGHT of where the path lands, is Chehalis, not this.
hazards: Unmarked, unmaintained climbers' path with no signage

approach_variants.name: North Exfo approach to lower Salami Slab
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
approach_variants.notes: As for Snagglepuss: FS 2060 south from Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, and then an unmarked climbers' path to the west-facing slabs below the north end of Exfoliation Dome. There is no maintained trail; the slab is visible from Three O'Clock Rock, which is the easiest way to identify the objective before walking in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Chehalis is on the RIGHT side of lower Salami Slab — right of the point where the approach path lands, which is where Snagglepuss begins.

The character is the confirmation: this is a long clean slab pitch that is nearly all friction, with very few knobs to pull on. If you are linking slabby corridors toward a prominent overlap you have started on Snagglepuss instead.
hazards: Unmarked, unmaintained climbers' path

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; the gully and slab approach are miserable and slick when wet
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington take FR 2060 (Clear Creek) for five or six miles and bear RIGHT at the fork. Pass the Eightmile Creek trailhead parking and keep going as the road deteriorates; after roughly another 1.5 miles it becomes effectively undriveable and there is a turnaround. The last couple of miles of the Copper Creek road have gone unmaintained for well over a decade, so how far you drive depends on the year and your clearance.

On foot: follow the old road extension for about half a mile, where it drops onto an older mining road. Where that ends, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left and follow the main fork up to a series of three waterfalls.

At the waterfalls, take a sharp RIGHT into a brushy rocky tunnel. This is the single move people get wrong. Continuing upward alongside the waterfalls leads into trouble, and there can be flagging near the waterfalls that was not put there by climbers — do not follow tape uphill past the tunnel. Through the tunnel, a tiny gully heads up and right into the maples and opens into a larger gritty slab gully that is followed all the way to the rock.

About 3 miles and 1,500 feet from the end of the driveable road, roughly two hours in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The staging area is a few hundred feet BELOW the steeper rock, and the honest answer is that there is no dramatic landmark. What distinguishes it is vegetation: a few small cedars standing straight up, where everything above that point looks bushier and scrappier. If the trees around you are upright cedars rather than bushes, you are at the staging area.

The routes start on the right-hand side of the buttress. From the staging area you scramble up and rightward; from there Dreamer and Safe Sex carry on past the dihedral to the right and up the apron below the buttress proper.

Easy scrambling and low-angle apron before anything that feels like climbing is CORRECT on this buttress — it is not evidence you are below the wrong feature.
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls and continuing uphill — the recorded way parties get into trouble here
Non-climber flagging near the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Long unmaintained road; no cell service in the valley

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Dreamer approach. FR 2060 from the Mountain Loop Highway, RIGHT at the fork, past the Eightmile Creek trailhead, and on until the road quits about 1.5 miles later.

Walk the old road extension half a mile until it drops to an older mining road, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left, follow the main fork to three waterfalls, and then take the sharp RIGHT into the brushy rocky tunnel. Do not keep going up beside the waterfalls, and do not trust flagging you find near them. Through the tunnel a small gully leads up and right into the maples and opens into a larger gritty gully that runs to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrive at the staging area a few hundred feet below the steeper rock — recognisable only by a handful of small cedars standing upright where the vegetation above is bushier.

Safe Sex shares this staging with Dreamer: scramble up and rightward, then continue past the dihedral to the right and up the apron beneath the buttress proper. Parties record easy, enjoyable scrambling to reach the first real pitch, followed by a 5.7 slab pitch with spaced protection — so a long scrambly warm-up before the rope comes out is CORRECT.
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls
Non-climber flagging near the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Runout slab climbing from the first pitch onward

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of Green Giant Buttress. FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway for five or six miles, RIGHT at the fork, past the Eightmile Creek trailhead, then on until the road stops being driveable roughly 1.5 miles later.

On foot: old road extension for half a mile, drop onto the older mining road, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left, follow the main fork to three waterfalls, then sharp RIGHT into the brushy rocky tunnel and up the gritty slab gully to the rock. Continuing up alongside the waterfalls instead of taking the tunnel is the classic mistake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Reach the same staging area used by the whole buttress — a few hundred feet below the steeper rock, marked only by small upright cedars against bushier growth above.

Urban Bypass is a short bolted variation on the buttress rather than a separate approach; it is climbed off the same right-side start as the Dreamer lines, so find the staging area first and pick the line off the apron from there. It is the only sport-bolted option here, so a line of bolts is the discriminator against the trad lines beside it.
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Long unmaintained road; no cell service

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the Roan Wall base commonly holds residual avalanche snow well into the climbing season
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington turn south on Madison Ave, follow it to a T, turn right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and follow it to where a washout gates it off.

Walk the old roadbed. A landslide crossing comes about five minutes in and is flagged. The original road end is about 30-40 minutes from the car. Carry on along the old trail for another 20-30 minutes.

The turn-off is a landmark, not a sign: a large dry streambed roughly 50 feet wide and full of white boulders. This is the LAST turnoff before the Squire Creek trail swings south out of the valley toward Squire Creek Pass — if the trail starts climbing away southward, you walked past it.

Drop about 200 feet down the streambed, trending left into alders, where an informal path becomes visible. Follow that upvalley for roughly 30 minutes to a ford of Squire Creek. Past a small creek channel the trail fades; keep following the underground creek bed and it opens into the basin, about two hours from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In the basin, keep following the creek bed until a thin, boulder-filled watercourse comes down directly out of the wall above you. That watercourse is obvious once it appears, and scrambling up it puts you at the base of Roan Wall — the big red slab split by a prominent corner system.

The overhung boulder called Martha's Place, which carries sport routes on its underside, sits near the base and is the bivy; if you can see it you are in the right place.

Critical: the first two pitches are approach pitches, not the route. An obvious bolted 80-foot 5.8 slab, then a low-fifth 150-foot groove, come BEFORE the climbing proper. Easy bolted slab at the bottom of a 5.11 route is correct here, not evidence you are on the wrong line. Center Stage takes the middle of the wall; the harder crux slab pitch is high (P7), not low.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek — difficult in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the season
Faint informal path through alder; the trail fades entirely in the basin

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the base commonly holds residual avalanche snow
approach_variants.notes:
Darrington: Madison Ave south to a T, right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, to the washout gate.

Old roadbed on foot — flagged landslide crossing about five minutes in, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes more on the old trail to a large dry streambed about 50 feet across and full of white boulders. That streambed is the Waterfall Basin turn-off and it is the last one before the trail heads south for Squire Creek Pass.

Descend the bed about 200 feet, trend left into alders to pick up an informal path, follow it roughly 30 minutes to the ford of Squire Creek, then continue as the trail fades along the underground creek bed until the basin opens up, about two hours from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Follow the creek bed in the basin until a thin boulder-filled watercourse drops directly out of the wall; scramble it to the base of Roan Wall, the large red slab with the prominent corner system. Martha's Place, the huge overhung boulder with sport routes under it, sits near the base.

Stage Right is the right-hand of the two Roan Wall lines; Center Stage takes the middle. Both share the same base and the same two easy approach pitches — a bolted 80-foot 5.8 slab and a low-fifth 150-foot groove — before the real climbing starts, so easy ground at the bottom is expected.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base
Path fades in the basin

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.season: Summer; east-facing, so morning sun and afternoon shade, but the base is often buried in leftover avalanche snow
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington, Madison Ave south to the T, right on Darrington Street into Squire Creek Road, drive to the washout gate.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing (about five minutes), reach the original road end in 30-40 minutes, then continue 20-30 minutes on the old trail to a large dry streambed about 50 feet wide and full of white boulders — the Waterfall Basin turn-off, and the last turn-off before the trail leaves the valley southward.

Down the bed about 200 feet, left into alder to find the informal path, roughly 30 minutes upvalley to the ford of Squire Creek, then along the fading trail and the underground creek bed into the open basin at about two hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the prominent rib sitting ABOVE the Martha's Place bivy boulder, immediately left of Roan Wall's big slab and its major waterfall streak. Standing at Martha's Place and looking up at a defined rib rather than a broad red slab is the confirmation.

The rib's position left of the waterfall is what gives it some shelter from snow and debris coming off the slab above — so if you are stood under the wet streak itself you are on Roan Wall, not this.

The base is commonly buried under leftover avalanche snow for much of the season, so expect to be starting off snow rather than dirt.
hazards: Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the climbing season
Debris and meltwater shed off the slab above
Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford drops and the basin snow has gone
approach_variants.notes:
Darrington to the end of Squire Creek Road (Madison Ave south, T, right on Darrington Street). The road is gated by a washout.

On foot: old roadbed, flagged landslide crossing at about five minutes, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes more to the wide dry streambed full of white boulders. That is the turn-off, and it is the last one before the trail heads south out of the valley.

Descend the bed roughly 200 feet, trend left into the alders to find the informal path, follow it about 30 minutes to the ford of Squire Creek, then keep on as the trail fades along the underground creek bed until the basin opens, about two hours from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
All the Waterfall Basin lines are found from the same reference: follow the creek bed until the thin boulder-filled watercourse comes down directly from the wall, scramble it, and you are at the base with Martha's Place — the huge overhung boulder — beside you.

From there pick the line off the wall. Note the route name is a bird reference, not a closure: no raptor closure is recorded for this basin in any source consulted, so do not read the name as a seasonal restriction.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Path fades entirely in the basin
Residual avalanche snow at the base early in the season

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low
approach_variants.notes: As for the rest of Waterfall Basin: Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, the old roadbed past a flagged landslide crossing, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes to a wide dry streambed full of white boulders. Down the bed about 200 feet, left into alders onto an informal path, 30 minutes upvalley, ford Squire Creek, then along the fading trail into the basin at roughly two hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is a short sport route in the basin rather than a wall route, and the reference point is Martha's Place — the enormously overhung boulder near the base of Roan Wall which carries the basin's sport climbing on its underside.

So you are looking DOWN at a boulder, not up at a thousand-foot slab. If you have scrambled the boulder-filled watercourse and are racking a rack for a wall you are on the wrong objective; this is at the bivy.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer; the boot track is steep and dirty and the saddle bivy is snow-free only in high summer
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington go south on Madison Ave to a T, right onto Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and drive to the washout that gates it.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing and on toward the old trailhead. The South Face turn-off is a made object, not a natural feature: look for TWO CUT LOGS, one on either side of the road, with old logging cable visible. At those logs turn right onto a well-beaten boot track.

The boot track drops to the creek for a ford, then climbs steeply through old-growth forest. The upper part is steep and dirty before it breaks out into open grassland. Around three hours from the trailhead to the main bivy.

This is a different turn-off from Waterfall Basin, which is further along at the wide white-boulder streambed. Two cut logs with cable = South Face; 50-foot streambed of white boulders = Waterfall Basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The reference point for the whole South Face is the grassy saddle bivy, and Concerto is the route that starts at it — the saddle sits near this route's start, which is why every other line here is described relative to it. A second, smaller saddle lies about ten minutes west along the wall; if you are at a small saddle with no route starting off it you are at the wrong one.

Standing at the main saddle, the granite apron of the South Face runs out in front of you. Concerto starts off that apron at the saddle itself. If you are crossing the apron away from the saddle you are heading for Nature's Way; if you are ascending class 4 ramps to a dihedral you are on the Primal Scream / Miracle Ramps side.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek on the boot track
Steep, dirty ground in the upper forest
Long approach with no maintained trail above the cut logs

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer; saddle bivy is a high-summer camp
approach_variants.notes:
Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, then the old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing.

The South Face turn-off is marked by two cut logs lying either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right there onto a well-beaten boot track, ford the creek, and climb steeply through old growth — steep and dirty near the top — until it opens into grassland and the grassy saddle bivy. About three hours from the trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree in it, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall. That dirt ledge is the start.

The small tree in the shallow dihedral is the discriminator. Miracle Ramps uses the same class 4 ramps but leads to a dihedral and then a starting wall ledge that it shares with this route's upper start, and the two only diverge higher; Nature's Way goes the other way, crossing the apron past Concerto's start to two-bolt ring anchors on the opposite wall.

This is an old-school ridge ramble: lichened overlaps and dirt-filled cracks low down are CORRECT here, not evidence of being off route. The crux does not arrive until pitch 9.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep, dirty forest on the upper boot track
Class 4 ramp scrambling to reach the start

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Squire Creek Road out of Darrington to the washout gate and walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing.

Turn right at the two cut logs with old logging cable onto the well-beaten boot track, ford the creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — steep and dirty higher up — into open grassland and the grassy saddle bivy, around three hours from the trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the grassy saddle bivy, go up class 4 ramps to a dihedral, then on to the starting wall ledge — the same ledge Primal Scream uses.

So you and a Primal Scream party would rack up in the same place: this route is a variation on the first six pitches of the older Primal Scream, up the right side of the central buttress, and finishes at its own summit anchor. Sharing the start is correct, not a mistake.

The confirmation higher is the four-bolt smeary crux the route is named for; if you never reach a bolted smearing section you have drifted onto the Primal Scream line proper.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Class 4 ramp scrambling to reach the start
Steep dirty forest below the grassland

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer
approach_variants.notes: Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing, then right at the two cut logs with old logging cable onto the boot track. Ford the creek, climb steeply through old growth into open grassland, and reach the grassy saddle bivy at about three hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross the granite apron, passing the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer, and carry on to two-bolt ring anchors on the OPPOSITE wall. Those ring anchors are the start.

The two discriminators are direction and hardware: you walk across the apron rather than up ramps, and you are looking for ring anchors rather than a bolt or a dirt ledge. Going up class 4 ramps from the saddle instead puts you on Primal Scream or Miracle Ramps.

The route's own payoff feature — the soaring hand crack above the apron — is visible from the apron, so sight it before committing.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest below the grassland
Exposed apron crossing

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington take Squire Creek Road to the washout that gates it, then walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing.

The South Face turn-off is two cut logs, one either side of the road, with old logging cable visible — turn right there onto the well-beaten boot track. It drops to a ford of the creek, then climbs steeply through old growth, steep and dirty near the top, into open grassland. The main grassy saddle bivy is about three hours from the trailhead, with a second smaller saddle roughly ten minutes further west along the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Get to the right saddle first. The main grassy saddle sits at the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer and is the reference every South Face line is described from; the smaller saddle ten minutes west is a different camp.

From the saddle the grey granite apron of the South Face is in front of you and the individual lines are picked off it. This route takes a dihedral with a lieback/stemming crux on pitch 2 and a delicate smearing finger traverse on pitch 3, sandwiched between easier friction above and below — so easy friction on pitch 1 is CORRECT here, not a sign you are on the wrong line. Protection is a mix of hand-drilled bolts on the faces and gear in the dihedral and cracks; a face with no gear placements at all is not this route.

The sources consulted do not give a ground-level marker specific to this line beyond the wall and the saddle reference — confirm against the wall topo before committing.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest on the upper boot track
Hand-drilled bolts of unknown age on the face sections

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.season: Summer
approach_variants.notes:
Squire Creek Road out of Darrington to the washout gate, then the old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing.

Turn right at the two cut logs with old logging cable onto the well-beaten boot track. Ford the creek, climb steeply through old-growth forest — the upper section is steep and dirty — and break out into grassland at the grassy saddle bivy, roughly three hours from the trailhead. A second, smaller saddle lies ten minutes west along the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The main grassy saddle, at the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer, is the reference point for the whole South Face; the smaller saddle further west is not it.

From the saddle the grey granite apron runs out below the wall and the lines are picked off it. Rock here is generally clean slab with cracks that can be dirt-filled low down — dirty cracks near the ground are normal on this face and are not evidence you are off route.

The sources consulted give no ground-level marker unique to this line, so identify it off the wall topo from the saddle rather than from anything underfoot.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest on the upper boot track

approach_variants.name: Olney Pass, old road walk and the two cairns
approach_variants.season: Dry summer days only, and DAYLIGHT ONLY — the PUD roads around Spada Reservoir are open sun-up to sun-down and you must register at the self-check kiosk on the way in
approach_variants.notes:
From US 2 at Sultan, turn onto Sultan Basin Road at the last stoplight. It is paved for around ten to eleven miles and then becomes well-graded gravel; carry on to Olney Pass and the Spada Reservoir area, about thirteen miles in.

Stop at the kiosk at Olney Pass and register your vehicle — the basin is Snohomish County PUD land with sun-up to sun-down access, and this is a standing rule rather than a temporary notice.

Continue to the fork and bear right around the southern tip of the reservoir. After about two miles cross a bridge and park in the first turnout on the left.

Walk the old road, which is eroded and overgrown and crosses numerous ravines where culverts have washed out. It is largely level for 45-60 minutes. The two markers are cairns and they do different jobs: the FIRST cairn, just before a large and usually dry riverbed, marks the point where you get a view up the bed to the slabs and Static Peak. Cross the riverbed and find a SECOND cairn sitting on an old culvert — that one marks where the trail leaves the road and goes uphill.

Follow it uphill alongside the riverbed for 20-30 minutes to the base of the dome. A short fixed line protects the last steep step before the Online sector, and it deposits you on a thin sandy ledge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the sandy arrival ledge, look up and find the first bolt you can see anywhere on the wall. That bolt is Online's, and it sits almost exactly in the MIDDLE of the wall.

It is roughly 50 feet up, and the slab below it is low-angle — about 5.5. So a long, easy, unprotected-feeling run to the first bolt is CORRECT here and is not a sign you are below the wrong line.

This is not a sport crag: the bolts were placed between expected gear placements, so wide spacing between bolts on a 5.10 is normal. Corners over on the LEFT side of the wall belong to Epitaph, a shorter 5.9, not to this.
hazards: PUD gate hours — being caught inside after sun-down
Washed-out culverts and ravines on the old road
Short fixed line on the final steep step to the sector
Runout below the first bolt

approach_variants.name: Olney Pass, old road walk and the two cairns
approach_variants.season: Dry summer days, daylight only — PUD access around Spada Reservoir is sun-up to sun-down with self-registration at the Olney Pass kiosk
approach_variants.notes:
US 2 to Sultan, left onto Sultan Basin Road at the last stoplight, paved for ten or eleven miles then gravel, about thirteen miles total to Olney Pass. Register at the kiosk.

Carry on to the fork, bear right around the south tip of the reservoir, and after roughly two miles cross a bridge and park in the first turnout on the left.

Walk the old eroded, overgrown road, crossing ravines where the culverts have gone. It stays largely level for 45-60 minutes. The first cairn appears just before a large, usually dry riverbed and marks the view up the bed toward the slabs and Static Peak. Cross the riverbed and look for the SECOND cairn, which sits on an old culvert and marks where the trail leaves the road.

From there the trail climbs beside the riverbed for 20-30 minutes to the base of the dome.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The reference point on arrival is Online's first bolt — the first bolt visible from the ground, sitting almost exactly in the middle of the wall about 50 feet up over low-angle slab. Locate that, and you know where the middle of the wall is.

Lost Charms is a separate five-pitch line on the same dome and the sources consulted do not describe its own ground marker, so identify it off the wall relative to Online's centre-of-wall bolt rather than from anything at your feet. Do not assume the first bolt you see is yours.
hazards: PUD gate hours — sun-up to sun-down only
Washed-out culverts and ravines on the old road
Steep step with a short fixed line near the top of the approach

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, straight up from the tracks
approach_variants.season: Any dry day; the Lower Wall gets full sun when the sun is out
approach_variants.notes:
Leave US 2 at the Index turnoff, about 29 miles west of Stevens Pass, and drive into town. Take Avenue A west for roughly 0.6 miles to a small gravel parking area on the right, just before the road runs alongside the railway.

From the lot you cross the railway tracks — every approach at Index crosses them, and trains come through several times a day, so look both ways and expect to shout at your belayer.

Once over the tracks bear a little left and pick up the trail heading up toward the wall. The branch that turns RIGHT runs along the base of the Lower Wall to the harder ground; going STRAIGHT takes you to the Great Northern Slab. Two to five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Great Northern Slab is the low-angle left end of the Lower Town Wall, and the trail from the lot runs straight into it — do not turn left or right.

The start marker is a flat ledge carrying a 5.10c toprope problem. You want the CORNER just LEFT of that flat ledge.

The first pitch is 5.2 and it climbs rightward up a ramp and through some bushes, then straight up an easier ramp to two very large bolts — the old one-inch-diameter kind. Scrappy vegetated ground and a ramp that wanders right is CORRECT on pitch 1; it is not a sign you have started on the wrong feature. Steep clean crack climbing off the deck means you have walked too far right along the base.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach — active line, several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking area

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day; full sun when the sun is out
approach_variants.notes:
Index turnoff from US 2, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right just before the road parallels the railway.

Cross the tracks — an active line with several trains a day. Bear a little left off the crossing to find the trail up toward the wall, then take the branch that turns RIGHT, which runs along the base of the Lower Wall past the Great Northern Slab and on to the Main Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
City Park is the landmark for this whole section — the obvious, unmistakable crack splitting the Main Wall. Find it first; everything here is described from it.

Godzilla is the crack and corner system IMMEDIATELY RIGHT of City Park. Standing at the base, the start is a shallow right-facing groove/face, positioned just right of being directly beneath the City Park crack.

So if you are stood exactly under the obvious splitter you have gone one line too far left. Step right until you are under a right-facing corner system and that is it.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach — several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking area
Busy wall — queues and parties above you dropping gear

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes:
US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the road runs beside the railway.

Cross the active railway tracks, bear left off the crossing to the trail, then take the RIGHT branch that runs along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
City Park is itself the landmark of the Lower Town Wall — the obvious crack that every neighbouring route is located from. If you are looking for something subtle you are looking at the wrong wall.

Stand directly beneath the obvious crack. If the feature in front of you is a shallow right-facing groove or corner system you have drifted RIGHT onto Godzilla, which is the line immediately right of this one.

The second pitch of this route is also the standard way parties reach Slow Children, so expect traffic moving through the line above you.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Traffic on the pitches above — this is the busiest part of the wall

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, straight off the trail
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes:
Index turnoff from US 2, through town, Avenue A west roughly 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right just before the road parallels the railway. Cross the active railway tracks and pick up the trail on the far side.

This is one of the shortest approaches at Index — seconds from the parking area.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route starts right off the trail. You do not scramble up to it and you do not traverse along the base to reach it; if you are pushing through anything to get to a start you have gone past it.

It is the reference point used for locating Japanese Gardens, which starts roughly midway between here and Godzilla — so if the ground in front of you is a short left-facing dihedral, you have walked toward Japanese Gardens and are between the two.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Popular line — queues on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the tracks — active line, several trains a day — bear left to the trail and then take the RIGHT branch running along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Position it between two known things: this route starts roughly MIDWAY between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla. Godzilla is the corner system immediately right of the obvious City Park crack; Princely Ambitions starts straight off the trail.

The start itself is a short LEFT-facing dihedral with a 5.10a section, and the line then trends right and comes back left into a wide crack.

Negative marker that matters: from this same start you can trend right and stay right into Stern Farmer, a 5.12 corner. Drifting right and not coming back left puts you on a testpiece two number grades harder. Sagittarius is the line just LEFT of this one.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Drifting right into Stern Farmer at the start

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same start as the full Japanese Gardens: roughly midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla, beginning in a short left-facing dihedral at about 5.10a, then trending right and back left into a wide crack, stopping at the first anchor.

The error to avoid is the same one: trending right out of the start and staying right leads into Stern Farmer, a 5.12 corner. Sagittarius is the neighbouring line to the LEFT.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the road runs beside the railway. Cross the tracks, bear left to the trail, take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Sagittarius sits just LEFT of Japanese Gardens, which itself starts about midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla.

The useful cluster to hold in your head: from left to right you have Numbah Ten — the bolted dihedral — then Iron Horse and Sagittarius, which share an anchor, then Japanese Gardens.

So if the feature in front of you is a bolted dihedral you are one or two lines too far left; if it is a short left-facing dihedral at about 5.10a you have stepped right onto Japanese Gardens.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and follow the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Numbah Ten is the BOLTED DIHEDRAL, and it sits LEFT of both Sagittarius and Iron Horse.

Bolts in a corner are the discriminator here — almost everything around it on this part of the wall is gear-protected. The obvious groove at the base, left of Iron Horse, is the start; Amandla shares that start before diverging.

If you are under a line that shares its anchor with Sagittarius you are on Iron Horse, one line right.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail, take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Iron Horse sits in the tight cluster with Sagittarius and Numbah Ten and shares an anchor with Sagittarius.

The reliable marker is its neighbour: Numbah Ten is the BOLTED dihedral immediately LEFT of Iron Horse, and the obvious groove at the base of that dihedral belongs to Numbah Ten and Amandla, not to this. Step right off that groove.

Japanese Gardens is further right again, starting midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot just before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This starts AS FOR Numbah Ten, in the obvious groove LEFT of Iron Horse, and only becomes its own line higher up.

So the thing to find on the ground is Numbah Ten's bolted dihedral and the groove at its base. Sharing a start with an easier neighbour is correct here.

If you are under a line that shares an anchor with Sagittarius you have stepped right onto Iron Horse.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, then climbed into from below
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes to the base of the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This pitch does NOT start from the ground. Looking for a ground-level start is the error.

The normal way in is to climb Godzilla — the corner system immediately right of the obvious City Park crack — and then the second pitch of City Park, which deposits you at the base of this pitch.

Once there, the start is a flake in a left-facing corner: you either traverse into it or step straight onto it, place a small cam around 0.4, and make a hard move into finger locks in a right-facing corner. If you are stood on the deck at a left-facing corner you are somewhere else entirely.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Two pitches of climbing before you reach the start — committing

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Start as for Japanese Gardens — roughly midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla, in the short left-facing dihedral — and then trend RIGHT into the corner instead of coming back left.

So the ground marker is not this route's own; it is Japanese Gardens'. The divergence happens above the start, and getting it wrong in the other direction is how Japanese Gardens parties accidentally end up on a 5.12 corner.
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Railway tracks to The Country, then the Upper Town Wall trail
approach_variants.season: Dry days; the Upper Wall trail is steep and slick when wet
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Lower Town Wall lot (Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles) and cross the railway tracks as for the Lower Wall.

Rather than turning up to the Lower Wall, follow the tracks along to the far north end, past the Lower Wall, to the clearing at The Country. The landmark on the way is the huge tunnel door; you cut left by the Country area near it.

At the clearing, walk to the FAR RIGHT of it, near the start of the route GM, where there may be a notice board. From there an obvious path leads uphill.

Allow about 30 minutes; one account calls it a 50-minute walk through ferns and moss. It is short but very steep, with cliffy drop-offs beside the path — this is the part of Index where people get hurt walking.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Davis-Holland is IMMEDIATELY TO THE LEFT of the point where the standard approach trail arrives at the Upper Town Wall. It is the first thing you meet, not something you hunt for.

The start takes a corner that lies to the LEFT of a blank face — the blank face is the discriminator; the corner beside it is yours.

If you have kept walking uphill past the arrival point you are heading for the Sport Wall, which sits further up. The standard link-up continues into Lovin' Arms above, so the three pitches of Davis-Holland ending at a belay is correct, not the top.
hazards: Steep climbers' trail with cliffy drop-offs
Railway crossing and walking the tracks — active line, several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking

approach_variants.name: Railway tracks to The Country, Upper Town Wall trail, then climbed into
approach_variants.season: Dry days
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lower Town Wall lot cross the railway tracks and follow them north past the Lower Wall to the clearing at The Country, cutting left near the huge tunnel door. Go to the far right of the clearing, near the start of GM and a possible notice board, and take the obvious path uphill.

About 30 minutes, short and very steep with cliffy drop-offs beside the trail.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lovin' Arms is the standard continuation ABOVE Davis-Holland, not a ground start — the two together are the classic seven-pitch link-up of the Upper Town Wall.

So the base to find is Davis-Holland's: immediately LEFT of where the approach trail arrives at the wall, taking a corner left of a blank face. Climb the three Davis-Holland pitches and continue.

If you are casting around at the base of the Upper Wall for an independent start to this you will not find one.
hazards: Steep climbers' trail with cliffy drop-offs
Railway crossing and track walking
Committing — you are three pitches up before this route begins

approach_variants.name: Heart Lake Road kiosk pullout, trail 248 to 247
approach_variants.season: Year-round; Mount Erie is open all year and no seasonal raptor closure is currently in force
approach_variants.notes:
From I-5 take SR 20 west toward Anacortes and Deception Pass, trend right onto Campbell Lake Road, then right at the Lake Erie Grocery onto Heart Lake Road.

About an eighth of a mile (roughly 0.2 miles) north of the grocery there is a gravel pullout on the east side of Heart Lake Road with an information kiosk. That is the Main Wall parking.

Take trail 248, which enters the woods on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE GATE. Follow it 5-10 minutes to a T junction with trail 247. Turn RIGHT — this is the junction that decides your day, because turning LEFT here takes you along mostly flat ground past a bench to Shady Hollow and the New Millennium Wall instead.

After the right turn, walk 2-5 minutes watching for a less-travelled UNMARKED trail on the LEFT. Take it uphill into the woods. It climbs short rock steps and then enters a clearing that gives a clear view of the Headwall and Snag Buttress routes. Keep going uphill and stay RIGHT at the final fork — the left branch leads to Ramp Wall. Fifteen to twenty minutes total.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The trail meets the cliff at a prominent RIGHT-FACING CORNER, and that corner is the first pitch of Zig Zag. Where the path stops being a path is the route.

That corner is also the anchor point for the rest of Main Wall West — everything else here is found by walking along the base from it.

If you came out at a clearing looking across at a buttress rather than standing under a corner, you are still below the wall: carry on uphill and stay right at the fork.
hazards: Unmarked junction — the left turn off trail 247 is easy to walk past
Short rock steps on the approach path

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.season: Year-round; Mount Erie is open all year with no current raptor closure
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Mount Erie summit road (Ray Auld Memorial Drive, off Heart Lake Road just past the Lake Erie Grocery) and park at the LAST parking area before the summit, at a sharp left-hand turn of more than 90 degrees. It holds about six cars; if it is full, park at the upper lot and walk down, under five minutes.

From the pullout, contour downward and westward along grassy ledges and short rock steps. A short section through woods and then under the powerlines brings you out on top of a cliff looking over Lake Erie and the strait.

A low third-class ramp then descends to the wall. Some parties rappel in from trees or scramble exposed ground to hang topropes; walking the ramp to the base and leading the well-bolted routes is the normal way.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the bottom of the third-class ramp, turn LEFT for the lower tier of the wall.

Intimidator starts at the LOWEST POINT of the whole wall — that is the marker, and it is unambiguous underfoot: if the ground continues to drop away beside you, keep walking down.

The lower tier holds False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator. If you have scrambled up two distinct blocky fourth-class steps heading south you have gone up onto the upper tier, which is Tindall's Terror and Scarface.
hazards: Exposed contouring above a cliff top on the way in
Third-class ramp descent to the base
Small parking area — do not leave valuables in the car

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the last parking area before the Mount Erie summit, at a sharp left-hand bend on the summit road; it takes about six cars, and the upper lot is a sub-five-minute walk away if it is full.

Contour down and west on grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short belt of woods and under the powerlines, to the top of a cliff above Lake Erie. A low third-class ramp descends from there to the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the bottom of the ramp, turn LEFT along the lower tier. False Impressions is one of the lower-tier lines, alongside Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator.

The fixed reference on this tier is Intimidator, which starts at the lowest point of the wall — locate that and work along the base from it.

If you find yourself scrambling two blocky fourth-class steps southward you have left the lower tier for the upper one (Tindall's Terror, Scarface) and gone too far.
hazards: Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent to the base

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes: Park at the last lot before the summit on the Mount Erie summit road, at a sharp left-hand bend. Contour downward and west along grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short section of woods and under the powerlines, to the top of the cliff above Lake Erie. Descend the low third-class ramp to the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Turn LEFT at the bottom of the ramp for the lower tier, which holds False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator.

Use Intimidator as the datum: it begins at the lowest point of the wall. Everything on this tier is located by walking the base from there.

Going south past the lower tier over two blocky fourth-class scrambles puts you on the upper tier with Tindall's Terror and Scarface — a different set of routes.
hazards: Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent to the base

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes: Drive the summit road and park at the last parking area before the summit, at a sharp left-hand turn. Contour down and west on grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a strip of woods and beneath the powerlines, emerging on top of a cliff overlooking Lake Erie, then take the low third-class ramp down to the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left at the bottom of the ramp puts you on the lower tier: False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator, Terminator.

Intimidator's start at the wall's lowest point is the fixed reference for the tier; find that first, then work along the base.

Note the name collision at this crag — there is a Terminator here on the Powerline Wall and a separate The Terminator on Index's Dihedral Wall. If your topo shows a dihedral wall rather than a bolted tier above Lake Erie you are reading the wrong crag.
hazards: Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent to the base

approach_variants.name: Summit road, powerlines, then south to the upper tier
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes: Park at the last parking area before the Mount Erie summit, at the sharp left-hand bend on the summit road. Contour down and west along grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short belt of woods and under the powerlines, to the cliff top above Lake Erie, then descend the low third-class ramp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the bottom of the ramp, go LEFT and then keep heading SOUTH past the lower-tier routes (False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator, Terminator). Intimidator, at the wall's lowest point, is the marker you pass.

The confirmation is two distinct blocky FOURTH-CLASS scrambles: you have to do both to reach the upper tier. Having to scramble twice is correct here and is not evidence you have wandered off the approach.

Tindall's Terror and Scarface are the upper-tier routes. If you never scrambled, you are still on the lower tier.
hazards: Two fourth-class scrambles at the base with exposure below
Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent

approach_variants.name: Summit road, powerlines, then south to the upper tier
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes: Drive to the last parking area before the Mount Erie summit, at the sharp left-hand bend. Contour downward and west on grassy ledges and short rock steps, through woods and under the powerlines to the top of the cliff above Lake Erie, and descend the low third-class ramp to the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Left at the ramp base, then south along the lower tier and up two distinct blocky fourth-class scrambles to reach the upper tier, which holds Scarface and Tindall's Terror.

The lowest point of the wall, which is Intimidator's start, is the datum you leave behind — if you are stood at the lowest ground you are on the lower tier and have not yet done the scrambles.

Some parties instead rappel in from trees or make exposed scrambles to hang topropes on this wall; the described approach is to walk to the base and lead.
hazards: Two fourth-class scrambles at the base with exposure below
Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent

approach_variants.name: Up and left off the Main Wall trail
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the gravel pullout with the information kiosk on the east side of Heart Lake Road, about 0.2 miles north of the Lake Erie Grocery. Take trail 248 into the woods on the RIGHT of the gate, follow it 5-10 minutes to the T junction with trail 247, and turn right.

The Skyline Arete cliffs sit WEST of the Main Wall, and the way in is by trails that lead up and LEFT off the Main Wall trail (off 247), with some scrambling. This is a complex series of cliffs bordered by steep brush and gullies, so expect to be picking a line rather than following a built path.

Approaching from above, near the Powerline and Orange areas, involves rappels and is not recommended for this crag.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Skyline Arete starts at the FAR LEFT END of Black Lichen Slab — so the slab is the feature to identify first, and then you walk to its left-hand extremity.

The first climbing takes airy moves through the LEFT side of the prominent roof, then follows the RIGHT side of the arete above.

If you are heading through the right side of the roof, or are on a slab with no arete above it, you are on a neighbouring line. At 5.5 this is one of the easiest routes on the mountain — if the moves off the ground feel hard you are not on it.
hazards: Steep brush and gullies between the cliffs — this is the most complex ground at Mount Erie
Scrambling on the approach trails off 247
Approaching from above requires rappels and is discouraged
